title: Monopoly & Imperfect Competition (HL) Adventure 2: Price Discrimination
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet the three degrees of price discrimination.
meta_desc: Economics HL: first, second and third degree price discrimination.
final_note: You classified the three degrees of price discrimination with real examples.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Arthur Pigou (1920) defined three degrees.

1° (perfect): each buyer pays their maximum willingness to pay — captures full consumer surplus. Rare; bespoke auctions, haggling.

2°: prices vary with quantity — bulk discounts, two-part tariffs, off-peak fares.

3°: prices vary by group with different elasticities — student, senior, peak/off-peak rail.

Three conditions are needed.

1. Market power — must be a price-maker.
2. Segmentable markets — identifiable groups with different elasticities.
3. No arbitrage — cannot resell from low-price to high-price segment.

Price discrimination raises producer surplus and can raise total output above non-discriminatory monopoly — bringing buyers in who would otherwise be priced out.

Distribution: high-WTP buyers lose surplus; some low-WTP buyers gain access. Equity is ambiguous; efficiency may improve.
